name: The Tabu Tree of Ato Myojin Shrine

location.address: Ato Myojin Shrine, Numata-cho Ato, Asaminami-ku, Hiroshima (near 914 Ato, Numata-cho)

access: Free. The shrine grove is a city-designated natural monument on ordinary shrine grounds, open in the way shrine precincts generally are.
transport: Rural Asaminami-ku; reachable by bus toward Numata-cho Ato, about a 2 minute walk from the Kamihara stop per local sources. No detailed transit timetable confirmed.
verify_notes: Environment Ministry giant-tree survey (report_id 69346, surveyed 2000): girth 373cm, health good, owner category shrine/temple (社寺), facility 阿刀明神社 (Ato Myojin Shrine), Numata-cho Oaza Ato Aza Tonoyama, Asaminami-ku. Second, independent source: the shrine's grove (社叢) was designated a Hiroshima City natural monument on 1974-02-18 (per hiroshima-navi.or.jp and mogurin.or.jp, the city's own cultural-property record), which separately names a tabu tree (タブノキ) at 3.62m girth as 'the representative large tree of the area' (though the tabu itself is not formally part of the 1974 designation), alongside a sugi/cedar at 3.41m (see hir_019) and a koyamaki/umbrella pine at 2.57m and 2.20m (not in the ministry register, not published here). The two figures for the tabu (3.62m in 1974 vs 3.73m in the 2000 ministry survey) are consistent with modest growth over 26 years and are treated as the same tree. Shrine founding is traditionally dated to 852 AD (per omairi.club and hiroshima-navi), reorganised in 1837 when the old Ato Myojin merged with a Hachiman shrine; various trees (cedar, hinoki, ginkgo) are said to have been planted around that reorganisation, but no source ties this specific tabu to a planting date, so no age is claimed (avoiding a bridge claim). No evidence found of felling, damage or death; a separate old blog post title referencing 'a giant cedar that used to be there' at this shrine could not be fetched (403), so it is flagged rather than ignored, see hir_019 notes. Location: town-level geocode only (the shrine's own coordinates could not be resolved via Nominatim or Overpass); the shrine's street address is reported elsewhere as Numata-cho Ato 914, Asaminami-ku. Two independent sources satisfied for existence and species; age genuinely undocumented, page should ask the reader for a precise measurement/date if they have one.

name: The Cedar of Ato Myojin Shrine

location.address: Ato Myojin Shrine, Numata-cho Ato, Asaminami-ku, Hiroshima (near 914 Ato, Numata-cho)

access: Free. Same city-designated natural monument grove as hir_018 (the Tabu Tree of Ato Myojin Shrine), on ordinary shrine grounds.
transport: Rural Asaminami-ku; reachable by bus toward Numata-cho Ato, about a 2 minute walk from the Kamihara stop per local sources.
verify_notes: Environment Ministry giant-tree survey (report_id 69347, surveyed 2000): girth 410cm, health good, same shrine and grove as hir_018. Second source: the shrine grove's 1974 city natural-monument designation names a sugi/cedar at 3.41m girth (hiroshima-navi.or.jp, mogurin.or.jp); the growth from 3.41m (1974) to 4.10m (2000 ministry survey) is a plausible 26-year increase for a large cedar and is treated as the same individual, though this is an inference rather than a stated identity. A blog post titled '...and the story of a giant cedar that used to be there' (gikou2.seesaa.net/article/490310343.html) exists about this exact shrine grove and could not be fetched (403 Forbidden on two attempts); it may describe a DIFFERENT, now-dead cedar rather than this one, since the surviving cedar is independently documented in the 1974 and 2000 records above, but this should be checked by a future pass before treating the surviving cedar's continued presence as fully settled. Grove founding traditionally 852 AD, reorganised 1837; no source dates this specific cedar's planting, so no age is claimed. Location is town-level (shrine's own coordinates not resolved); reported street address elsewhere is Numata-cho Ato 914, Asaminami-ku.

name: The Cedar of Matsukasa Kannon's Inner Sanctuary

location.address: Matsukasa Kannon-ji Oku-no-in (inner sanctuary), Mount Matsukasa (374m), Kuchita-minami-cho, Asakita-ku, Hiroshima

access: Free, but a genuine hike: the temple's inner sanctuary sits on the summit area of Mount Matsukasa (374.3m), reached by a marked hiking trail from JR Tosaka Station (climbed and photographed as recently as 2019 per a hiking blog, though a 2018 landslide closed part of the original route and a detour is in use).
transport: JR Tosaka Station, then a hiking trail up Mount Matsukasa; no public transport reaches the temple itself.
verify_notes: Environment Ministry giant-tree survey (report_id 69363, surveyed 2000): girth 480cm, health good, owner category shrine/temple, facility 松笠観音 (Matsukasa Kannon), Koyo-cho Oda-Iwatsubo, Asakita-ku. Cross-checked: the temple has two parts, a main hall (Honin) in Tosaka Yamane, Higashi-ku, and an inner sanctuary (Oku-no-in) on Mount Matsukasa itself in Kuchita-minami-cho, Asakita-ku (confirmed via a 2019 hiking blog, arukurumen.com, and the temple's own Jimdo site, matsukasakanonji.jimdofree.com, Shingon sect, founded 1530); the register's town name (Koyo-cho Oda-Iwatsubo) and the confirmed Oku-no-in site (Kuchita-minami-cho) are both Asakita-ku localities close to the same mountain, so this is treated as the same site, but the exact match between the register's address text and the confirmed hiking-trail location is not textually perfect and a future pass should double check no separate 松笠観音 exists nearby. The hiking blog confirms the site is open, actively visited (2019, with a 2018 landslide detour still passable) and describes the temple buildings (Mizuko Kannon, Kobo Daishi's well, Shaka-do) but the excerpt fetched did not itself describe this specific cedar; no second source names the tree directly, so this is register-plus-site-corroboration rather than a tree-specific second source, and is flagged accordingly. A second registered tree at the same site, an Abemaki oak (Quercus variabilis) at 310cm girth, report_id 69364, is left as a lead (see leads file) rather than published separately, as a companion specimen at the same small mountaintop site. No evidence of felling or death found for either tree. Location is site-level only (OSM tags a 松笠観音寺 place-of-worship node here, but not tree-level), never confirmed.

name: The Muku Tree of Kirihata Shrine
access: Free. Shrine grounds on a hillside about 100m east of Route 2, between JR Seno and Nakano-higashi stations; hitozato-kyoboku.com's own visit (2017) describes ordinary shrine access.
transport: Between JR Sanyo Main Line's Seno and Nakano-higashi stations; roughly a 10 to 15 minute walk from either.
verify_notes: Environment Ministry giant-tree survey (report_id 69374, surveyed 2000): species Muku (Aphananthe aspera), girth 300cm, health not recorded ('--'), owner category shrine/temple, facility 切幡神社 (Kirihata Shrine), Nakano-higashi 7-chome, Aki-ku. Second source found for the SHRINE but not this specific tree: hitozato-kyoboku.com's giant-tree catalogue documents a DIFFERENT tree at the same shrine, a great zelkova (大ケヤキ), 5.6m girth and 28m tall, designated together with the shii-forest grove behind the shrine as a Hiroshima City Natural Monument on 1974-02-18 under the name 'Kirihata Shrine's Great Zelkova and Shii Forest', with precise coordinates (34.41233N 132.58633E, converted from the page's degree-minute-second figures) matching the register's address exactly (Nakano-higashi 7-chome). This firmly confirms the shrine's existence, public designation and location, but the zelkova is a different, larger, separately-registered tree (not part of this pass's 24 target report_ids; NOTE FOR A FUTURE PASS: this zelkova appears to be an uncaptured lead worth adding, official measurements 5.6m girth / 28m height / natural monument since 1974, coordinates above). No independent source specifically describes the muku. No evidence of felling or death for the muku. Coordinates used are the shrine's own surveyed location (from the zelkova's natural-monument record), so site-level, not tree-level for the muku itself.
